name: Times club monthly special crossword No 20,238

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, number freed: 1 down to 2); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unusual aroma, etc, as TV interviewee speaks?

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the normal order, so the letters that follow are rearranged

blocks.note: all eight letters of the two words, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: A smell in a television studio puts a guest off as they talk on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A person interviewed on television often addresses the lens directly, which is how the phrase is used of speech on screen.

clue.text: Longer spell of fine weather’s third month — ace for a Japanese city

indicators.note: third points to the letter in the third position of the weather word

blocks.note: OK means fine, and this is its fuller spelling
the third letter of weather
M is an abbreviation for month
A is the card abbreviation for ace

explanation.surface: A long run of sunny days in March gives a great reason to visit Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell of fine weather' looks like sunshine, but 'spell' means spelling: OKAY is the longer spelling of OK.
explanation.definitionFit: Okayama is a prefectural capital in western Honshu, known for its castle and Korakuen garden.

clue.text: Rugby players, a reserve, with half back, repeatedly supporting team in second half

indicators.note: only the second half of the team word is kept and its first half is lost
half back means one half of the reserve word is turned round while the other stays
in a down answer, supporting means sitting underneath, so these pieces come below

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
to book is to reserve
an instruction, not letters: the altered reserve word is used twice

explanation.surface: A rugby coach picks a substitute scrum-half who keeps coming on to support the side after the break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half back' looks like the rugby position, but it means turning round one half of the word only. In a down answer the supporting pieces sit below.
explanation.definitionFit: Amabokoboko is the Zulu nickname for South Africa's national rugby union side, the Springboks.

clue.text: Praise old singer cutting disc

indicators.note: cutting means removing, so the disc letter is taken out of the singer

blocks.note: ex means former, old
an alto is a singer with a low voice
O is round like a disc

explanation.surface: Applauding a veteran vocalist who is recording a record.
explanation.definitionFit: To exalt someone is to glorify or extol them highly, the same as giving them great acclaim.

clue.text: Motoring organisation in another limitless trip: it’s got a huge bill

indicators.note: in places one motoring body inside the other
limitless means without its outer edges, so only the inner letters of the journey word remain

blocks.note: the RAC, Royal Automobile Club, is a British motoring organisation
the AA, Automobile Association, is another British motoring organisation
the inner letters of trip

explanation.surface: A breakdown service on an endless journey runs up a massive charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAC and the AA are Britain's two big breakdown-recovery clubs. 'Huge bill' sounds like an invoice, but it is a beak.
explanation.definitionFit: An aracari is a small South American toucan, a bird with an enormous colourful beak.

clue.text: A dance party collects starchy food for Aussie

indicators.note: to collect is to gather up and hold, so the party word wraps round the dance word

blocks.note: taken as written
a do is an informal word for a party
a jig is a lively folk dance

explanation.surface: A party where people dance also lays on potatoes or similar for an Australian guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aussie' here is slang for Australian, signalling a word from Australian English rather than a general one.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjigo is a yam native to Western Australia whose tuber was eaten as a staple root by Aboriginal people.

clue.text: Perennial sufferings besetting island people

indicators.note: to beset is to surround on all sides, so the sufferings word goes round the rest

blocks.note: aches are pains or sufferings
I is the abbreviation for island
men are people

explanation.surface: Endless hardships afflicting the inhabitants of an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perennial' looks like an adjective for the sufferings, but it is the noun: a plant that lives for years.
explanation.definitionFit: Achimenes is a genus of tropical American flowering plants that regrow from rhizomes each year, so one is a perennial.

clue.text: Law finding politician out of bounds

indicators.note: out of means removed from, so the politician's letters are taken from bounds

blocks.note: bounds are leaps
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: A legal rule shows that a politician has overstepped the mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of bounds' reads as a phrase for straying too far; 'bounds' is the noun for jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Jus is Latin for a legal right or a body of legal principles, used in phrases like jus gentium.

clue.text: Attack old astrologer turning up unshaven

indicators.note: in a down answer turning up means the astrologer's name is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to go at someone is to attack them
John Dee was Elizabeth I's astrologer and magician

explanation.surface: Going for an ancient stargazer who arrives with stubble.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone goateed wears a small pointed beard on the chin, so that part of the face has been left unshaved.

clue.text: Chap’s after two staples of “learning to read” sentence — one with a comprehension problem

indicators.note: after places the man's word behind the earlier pieces in the line

blocks.clueFragment: two staples of “learning to read” sentence
blocks.note: early readers learn 'the cat sat on the mat', whose two key nouns each with an article are a cat and a mat
chap is he, and the apostrophe s gives he's
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A child's reading primer sentence and a man who can't follow it.
explanation.walkthrough: The reading-primer sentence is the classic 'The cat sat on the mat'; its staples are A CAT and A MAT, then HE'S, I and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Acatamathesia is a medical term for being unable to understand spoken language, a disorder of grasping meaning.

clue.text: Clumsy American, good at logarithms, initially backward in addition

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of each of the words it follows
backward tells us to read the word for in addition from right to left

blocks.note: the first letters of good, at and logarithms
too means also, in addition

explanation.surface: An awkward American who is strong at maths is still behind in simple sums.
explanation.definitionFit: Galoot is North American slang for an awkward, ungainly or oafish person, especially a big lumbering man.

clue.text: Pound perhaps to dress old monsieur, returning in French silk

indicators.note: to dress something is to clothe it, so the poet's name goes round the two letters
returning means the combined poet and old monsieur letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: Ezra Pound was the American modernist poet
O is the standard abbreviation for old
M. is the abbreviation for monsieur
en is the French word for in

explanation.surface: Something about money and clothing an elderly Frenchman who comes home wearing silk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound perhaps' looks like money or weight, but it is the modernist poet. The reversal covers the poet and the two letters inside, not the French word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Armozeen is an old name for a heavy plain taffeta, usually black, originally from France and used for mourning gowns.

clue.text: Publicizes me sneakily dropping Charlie for one of the Germans

indicators.note: dropping means letting go of, so the Charlie letter is removed
doing something sneakily means acting deviously, so the remaining letters are moved about

blocks.note: the letters of both words
C is Charlie in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A person complains that someone is secretly broadcasting their affairs while leaving out Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for one' is a way of saying 'for example', and 'of the Germans' asks for it in German.
explanation.definitionFit: Zum Beispiel is German for 'for example', the phrase behind the common abbreviation z.B. in that language.

clue.text: As certain Cossacks kill, or blunder defending area in borders

indicators.note: borders means the two letters for in form an edge on either side of the area letter

blocks.note: zap is slang for kill
taken as written
an own goal, a blunder by a defender in football
taken as written
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Cossack warriors weighing whether to kill or to make a mistake protecting land at the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blunder defending' is football: an own goal is the classic defender's error. 'in borders' means the word in forms the borders.
explanation.definitionFit: Zaporogian describes the Zaporozhian Cossacks who lived beyond the rapids of the Dnieper in Ukraine.

clue.text: Two managed firm, keeping books, elevating particular lines

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the books letters sit within the run
in a down answer elevating means lifting, so the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for two
ran a business is managed it
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A pair of executives ran a company that kept accounts and promoted some specific product lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'books' in a cryptic often means the Old or New Testament. 'Lines' is the definition in its poetic sense, verse lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Octonarii are verse lines of eight metrical feet in Latin poetry, a specific kind of line in prosody.

clue.text: Garment for the female aforesaid improperly reveals back

indicators.note: reveals means a run of letters is exposed inside the words before it
back tells us that the exposed run is read from right to left

blocks.note: the run spans the end of aforesaid and the start of improperly

explanation.surface: A woman's dress, already mentioned, is cut so low it shows her back.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a revealing dress showing a back; both words have mechanical jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A midi is a skirt or dress reaching to mid-calf, an item of clothing worn mostly by women.

clue.text: Henry V’s contemptuous gesture, neglecting odd parts of kingdom

indicators.note: neglecting the odd positions leaves only the even letters, second, fourth and so on

blocks.note: the even letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A king rudely gesturing while ignoring stray corners of his realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry V' is Shakespeare's play, not the king; the gesture comes from Pistol in that play.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Henry V Pistol says 'figo for thy friendship', a fig being an obscene snap of the fingers in scorn.

clue.text: Ironies rampant in one improving atmosphere through negativity?

indicators.note: rampant means running wild, so the letters break out of their order

blocks.note: the letters of the word

explanation.surface: A cynic, full of sarcasm, claims to lift the mood by being negative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'improving atmosphere' sounds like cheering up a room, but it means the air; 'negativity' refers to negative ions.
explanation.definitionFit: This device freshens indoor air by charging particles with negative ions so that dust and pollen settle out.

clue.text: Wasting time, I must abandon “Lincolnology”?

indicators.note: abandon means leave behind, so the following letter is dropped from the study

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
a jokey coinage: the science of Abe, Abraham Lincoln's first name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone frittering away hours who should give up their study of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasting time' reads as one phrase; only 'Wasting' is the definition and 'time' gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabescence is the gradual bodily decline of an emaciating illness, a medical word for wasting away.

clue.text: First meals casually halved, then one restricts wife’s US beer

indicators.note: halved means cut to half its length, so the back half of the word for meals is dropped
restricts means confines, so the wife letters are held within the surrounding pieces

blocks.note: brekkies is British slang for breakfasts
W is the abbreviation for wife, with the apostrophe s
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone eats half a breakfast, then cuts down on their partner's American lager.
explanation.walkthrough: Brekkies is casual British for breakfasts; its first half BREK plus I wraps W'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Brewski is an informal American word for a beer, a jokey variant of brew with a mock-Slavic ending.

clue.text: A hundred personnel at the double taking next to no time

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
HR, human resources, is the personnel department
on means taking, as in on drugs, and at the double asks for it twice

explanation.surface: A hundred staff rush to do something in a flash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the double' looks like hurrying, but it doubles ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronon is a hypothetical smallest indivisible unit of time, a tiny fraction of a second.

clue.text: Nun I once bumped into an unfamiliar woman

indicators.note: something bumped is jolted and knocked about, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters of all three words

explanation.surface: A sister from a convent tells of colliding with a stranger.
explanation.definitionFit: Inconnue is the French feminine for a stranger, used in English for a female person nobody knows.

clue.text: Tea mostly taken with right grub

definitions.note: verb: to clear land by digging up roots

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter of the tea word goes

blocks.note: Assam is a strong Indian black tea
RT is an abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Having a cup of tea along with some decent food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like a noun for food, but it is a verb meaning to dig up.
explanation.definitionFit: To assart is to clear woodland for farming by uprooting trees and bushes, an old forestry term.

clue.text: Fifty per cent cut in publicity used by record label

indicators.note: in a down answer the record label word is used to follow on from the publicity word

blocks.note: an ad is an advertisement, publicity
EMI is a British record label

explanation.surface: A half share of advertising money goes to a record company.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived phrase means by halves or half-and-half, so it equals a half share.

clue.text: Trouble with PR is, there is no room for sport!

indicators.note: to trouble is to disturb, so the letters that follow are thrown out of order

blocks.note: every letter of these five words

explanation.surface: A complaint that public relations has crowded out any space for games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no room for sport' reads as one phrase; 'no' belongs to the letters and 'room for sport' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sphaeristerion was a hall in ancient Greek gymnasia or houses set aside for ball games and exercise.

clue.text: It’s a puzzle with anagram form for which tips needed

definitions.note: an exclamation saying that something is puzzling

indicators.note: tips here are the final ends of the words, so their last letters are taken

blocks.note: the last letters of with, anagram and form

explanation.surface: A puzzle that needs hints because of its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: This interjection is the sound people make when they are pondering, doubtful or baffled by something.

clue.text: Odd to put on uniform? The first thing asked maybe in Chinese city

indicators.note: in an across answer, putting one piece on another places it after it

blocks.note: U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
rum means odd or strange in British slang
Q1, question one, with the numeral read as I

explanation.surface: Wondering whether it is strange to dress in uniform, the first query you might raise.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum is old-fashioned British for odd. Q1 is question one, the first thing asked, with 1 standing in for I.
explanation.definitionFit: Urumqi is the capital of Xinjiang in north-west China, said to be the city furthest from any sea.

clue.text: Iodine brought in as broken arm is for cutting off?

indicators.note: brought in means placed inside, so the element letter goes within the phrase for a broken arm's state

blocks.note: a broken arm is held in a sling
I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: A medic adds iodine to a fractured arm and wonders whether it must be amputated.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that 'cutting off' means isolating, as on an island, not amputating the arm.
explanation.definitionFit: To inisle is to put on an island, so it means isolating or separating something from its surroundings.
